title: a capability read inside a callback handed to a higher-order call charges the enclosing function's row, so a top-level call to it is still an unsatisfied requirement
notes: specification/requirements.mdx, 'Inference': 'Requirement inference MUST be transitive through ordinary calls.' `keys.map(cb)` calls `cb` synchronously, inside `readAll`, before `readAll` returns — so the capability is read during `readAll`'s own execution and belongs to `readAll`'s row. Until 2026-08-26 both backends deleted it at the callback boundary: `readAll` published `requirements: []`, and because the top-level unsatisfied-requirement check is computed FROM the row, the bare top-level call on line 11 was certified. The declared diagnostic is therefore doing two jobs at once, and the second is the reason the case is written this way round rather than as a row assertion. A row is not observable through a `diagnostics` expectation on either backend — and it cannot be read out of the Go fork at all, whose CompileResult protocol carries diagnostics, artifacts and `emitSkipped` and no rows — so the only way to state 'the row is `[Reader]` and not `[]`' in a form both backends can answer is to put the row somewhere a rule reads it. SMITHERS2102 is that place: an empty row produces NO diagnostic here, so the presence of this one at this position is the row. Note what makes the callback boundary the interesting one rather than an arbitrary one: it is already modelled for two other channels — a fallible callback is refused (`SMITHERS1303`) and an async callback is refused (`SMITHERS1404`) — so the requirement channel was the one channel not wired to a boundary the compiler already walks. WHAT THIS DELIBERATELY DOES NOT PIN: `messageContains` (one capability in the program, nothing wrong-but-plausible for a refusal to name, and the two backends render a row set differently — see `a-top-level-capability-read-is-rejected` for the full reasoning); and the other fifteen callback POSITIONS the implementations' own tests enumerate — an object-literal property, an array-literal argument, a `new` argument, a named function passed by reference — of which this is the builtin higher-order one. It also does not pin the two recorded residuals: a closure RETURNED from a function and a closure pushed into a module-level array still publish `[]` on both backends, because propagation is the wrong tool for a requirement needed at a later time, and `requirements.mdx, 'Inference'` leaves the encoding of a row on a function TYPE explicitly open. VERIFIED LOAD-BEARING, not assumed: mutating the declared code from SMITHERS2102 to SMITHERS2106 turns the case red on BOTH backends with the code diff printed, and the file was restored byte-identically (sha256 16671c876cd810e2a87cc21e6e62970c7f107f8dfabddeee21fbc405f393938b before and after). The paired positive control is `a-capability-read-inside-a-callback-charges-the-caller` — the same program with a Layer around it — which must keep compiling and RUNNING.
